cards.definitions:
The dimension \(n\geq1\) and a finite list of regions \(H_1,\ldots,H_p\) are given explicitly. The regions form a disjoint, exhaustive partition of \(\mathbb R^n\). Each region is a convex rational polyhedron specified by finitely many strict or non-strict rational linear inequalities. On integer points of region \(H_j\), the map is \(f(x)=A_jx+b_j\), where \(A_j\in\mathbb Z^{n\times n}\) and \(b_j\in\mathbb Z^n\). These integer coefficients guarantee an integer successor. There are no rounding operations or congruence tests.

All integer constants and rational numerators and denominators are written in binary. The input includes all regions, matrices, vectors and the starting and target vectors. Validity of the partition is a promise. The number of regions and coefficient magnitudes are not fixed constants.

Set \(f^0(x_0)=x_0\) and \(f^{t+1}(x_0)=f(f^t(x_0))\). Reachability includes time zero. The question concerns one given initial vector, unlike mortality, which requires every integer starting vector to reach zero.

“Recursively enumerable complete” means that yes-instances can be recognized by a procedure that halts when a target is found, but no total decision procedure exists; every recursively enumerable decision problem computably reduces to this one. PSPACE-completeness is for polynomial space in the total binary input length, with polynomial-time many-one reductions.

The source states the two-dimensional and one-dimensional classifications for target zero. They apply to any supplied integer target by translating coordinates: \(g(z)=f(z+y)-y\), with initial vector \(x_0-y\). Translation preserves the dimension, finite rational-polyhedral partition and integer affine coefficients, with polynomial encoding overhead. This is a direct consequence of the stated model, not a separate later theorem.
cards.answer_criterion: The historical universal decidability question has a negative answer by the two-dimensional recursively enumerable completeness result. The one-dimensional PSPACE-complete restriction remains decidable. A solver for rational linear maps, a fixed bounded region count or another restricted update family does not decide the full piecewise-affine integer problem.

cards.title: An elementary upper bound for vector-addition-system reachability
cards.formal: Do there exist a deterministic Turing-machine algorithm A and fixed integers h≥0 and c≥1 such that, for every explicitly encoded vector-addition-system reachability instance of bit length N, A decides exact reachability correctly within E_h((N+2)^c) steps, where E_0(x)=x and E_{j+1}(x)=2^{E_j(x)}? The constants and the single algorithm must work for all input dimensions and numerical values. This historical proposition is false.

source_formulation.text: Despite intense investigation during the last four decades, it is still an open problem whether an elementary complexity upper bound for the reachability problem exists.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 1

cards.why: Exact resource reachability is a basic verification problem that other decision tasks can encode. Its non-elementary complexity shows that decidability can coexist with worst-case costs beyond every fixed-height exponential tower, and that exact target matching can be much harder than merely accumulating enough resources.
cards.status_note: Checked 11 September 2026. The elementary-upper-bound proposition is false by the STOC 2019 / JACM 2021 non-elementarity result of Czerwiński, Lasota, Lazić, Leroux and Mazowiecki. The accepted journal manuscript’s Section 1 model and Theorem 6 match the unrestricted VAS reachability question on the original 2018 page. The later Ackermann-completeness result strengthens this resolution. Source and theorem matching were checked; proofs were not independently audited or formalized.

cards.definitions: An instance is a dimension d≥1, a nonempty finite list T of displacement vectors in ℤ^d, and initial and target vectors a,b∈ℕ^d, with ℕ={0,1,2,…}. A configuration is any vector in ℕ^d. From u one may take displacement t∈T exactly when every coordinate of u+t is nonnegative, obtaining u+t. The target is reachable if a finite sequence t₁,…,t_k∈T has a+∑_{i=1}^j t_i∈ℕ^d for every 0≤j≤k and a+∑_{i=1}^k t_i=b. Length k=0 is allowed. The input explicitly lists all coordinates, using binary integers with signs and separators; N is the total bit length. Dimension and list length are input parameters. A is one finite deterministic program and must halt with the exact yes/no answer on every valid instance. No random error, counter bound, polynomial-growth promise, zero-test instruction, or branching operation is included. An elementary running-time bound has some fixed tower height h as defined in the statement; the height cannot depend on the instance. Binary encoding fixes the presentation without changing whether any elementary bound exists, since translation to unary data has at most elementary size growth.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove or refute existence of the single uniform elementary-time decision algorithm quantified above. A refutation must exclude every fixed tower height and polynomial bottom exponent; showing that one algorithm or one fixed resource bound fails is insufficient. The published non-elementary lower bound supplies the negative resolution.

context_blocks.text: A counter vector can describe the quantities of several resources in a concurrent system. Every transition makes a fixed change, but cannot consume resources that are absent. The reachability question asks whether the system can finish with exactly the specified quantities, after any finite number of transitions.

For example, start at (2,0) with the single displacement (−1,2). The reachable vectors are (2,0), (1,2) and (0,4). The target (0,3) is not reachable, although (0,4) is coordinatewise at least as large. Replacing exact equality by that weaker comparison gives coverability, a different task.

Polynomial time, exponential time and a fixed stack of several exponentials are all elementary. Allowing the stack height to grow with input size is a qualitatively stronger resource bound. The old question asked whether some fixed height would suffice for every instance, rather than whether a particular implementation could be made faster.

The quoted 2018 question concerns unrestricted vector addition systems. The paper’s title refers to a special polynomial-growth subclass studied later in the article; imposing that restriction here would change the question. Likewise, a bound for one fixed low dimension would not establish the required uniform bound over all dimensions.

Czerwiński and coauthors proved a lower bound excluding elementary complexity, first presented at STOC 2019 and developed in a 2021 journal article. This is a limitation of the decision problem itself, not merely a demonstration of long runs or poor performance by an existing algorithm.

Subsequent work classified ordinary VAS/VASS reachability as Ackermann-complete. Finite control states and the state-free vector presentation are polynomially interreducible, so this later classification concerns the same unrestricted reachability task. The simpler non-elementarity theorem already settles the historical yes/no question recorded here.

The simpler non-elementarity theorem already settles the historical yes/no question recorded here.

cards.title: Milner’s completeness problem
cards.formal: Historical question, resolved affirmatively: for all regular expressions \(e,f\) over any finite action alphabet, does bisimilarity of their process interpretations imply that \(e=f\) is derivable in Milner’s proof system \(\mathrm{Mil}\)? Grabmayer’s LICS 2022 completeness theorem proves this implication for the full expression language defined below.

cards.definitions:
Fix a finite set \(A\) of action symbols. Expressions are finite terms
\[e::=0\mid1\mid a\mid(e+e)\mid(e\cdot e)\mid e^{*},\qquad a\in A.\]
Here 0 is deadlock, 1 is successful immediate termination, \(+\) is nondeterministic choice, multiplication is sequential composition, and star is iteration.

Define the immediate-termination predicate \(e\downarrow\) recursively. It holds for 1 and every \(e^{*}\), for \(e+f\) exactly when at least one summand terminates, and for \(e\cdot f\) exactly when both factors terminate. It does not hold for 0 or an action.

For each action \(a\), the transition relation \(\xrightarrow{a}\) is the least relation generated by the following rules. There is a transition \(a\xrightarrow{a}1\). Every transition of either summand is a transition of their sum. If \(e\xrightarrow{a}g\), then \(e\cdot f\xrightarrow{a}g\cdot f\) and \(e^{*}\xrightarrow{a}g\cdot e^{*}\). If \(e\downarrow\) and \(f\xrightarrow{a}g\), then \(e\cdot f\xrightarrow{a}g\). There are no other transitions.

A bisimulation is a relation \(B\) on expressions such that, whenever \((e,f)\in B\), they have the same termination predicate and each action transition from either expression can be matched by a transition with the same label from the other, with the resulting expressions again related by \(B\). The expressions are bisimilar if some such relation contains their pair. This is strong bisimilarity with observable successful termination. The constant 1 is not an action label or a silent transition in this semantics.

The proof system has these equation schemata, for arbitrary expressions \(e,f,g\):
\[\begin{aligned}
e+(f+g)&=(e+f)+g,&e+0&=e,\\
e+f&=f+e,&e+e&=e,\\
e\cdot(f\cdot g)&=(e\cdot f)\cdot g,\\
(e+f)\cdot g&=e\cdot g+f\cdot g,\\
1\cdot e&=e,&e\cdot1&=e,&0\cdot e&=0,\\
e^{*}&=1+e\cdot e^{*},&
e^{*}&=(1+e)^{*}.
\end{aligned}\]
It permits reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity of equality, and replacement of equals within each expression constructor. In addition, its fixed-point rule is
\[\frac{e=f\cdot e+g}{e=f^{*}\cdot g}\qquad\text{provided }f\not\downarrow.\]
The premise must itself be derivable; the side condition means that \(f\) cannot terminate immediately, as computed by the recursive predicate above. A proof is a finite derivation using these schemata and rules.

The system includes successful termination and unary star. Dropping 1 and replacing unary star by a binary iteration operator gives the separate one-free fragment. Dropping the fixed-point rule gives only the equational fragment, which is not the system in the question. Familiar language identities such as unrestricted left distributivity and \(e\cdot0=0\) must not be added: they need not preserve this branching process semantics.
cards.answer_criterion: The historical target is a completeness proof for every pair of bisimilar expressions in the full language and exactly the displayed proof system. A theorem only about equality of accepted languages, about a restricted fragment, or about a stronger proof system would not suffice. The cited theorem establishes the required implication.

context_blocks.title: Process equivalence retains branching information
context_blocks.text: Regular expressions can denote either languages or process behaviors. Bisimilarity compares which actions remain available after each step and preserves termination. Equality of accepted words alone is too coarse for this completeness question.

context_blocks.title: The 2021 source predates the full result
context_blocks.text: The source cites the earlier completeness theorem for one-free expressions and describes the full Milner problem as open. Its discussion of GKAT and a uniqueness axiom concerns a different expression language and should not replace the target here.

context_blocks.title: The full system is complete
context_blocks.text: Grabmayer’s Theorem 5.1 states completeness for Milner’s system on regular expressions, including 0, 1 and unary star. Soundness was already known. Together these facts identify derivable equality with bisimilarity for the stated process interpretation.

context_blocks.title: Later work treats the historical problem as solved
context_blocks.text: Kappé and Schmid’s 2025 paper explicitly attributes the resolution of Milner’s problem to Grabmayer, then studies a broader family of skip-free star algebras. This corroborates that the 2021 open-status label is stale.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
